lessons.title: Aggregate Functions
lessons.concept: Aggregate functions perform calculations on a set of rows and return a single value. Common aggregates include COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX. They are often used with GROUP BY to compute values per group.
lessons.formula: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) counts non-NULL values; SUM(col), AVG(col), MIN(col), MAX(col) operate on column values (NULL handling varies by function).
lessons.worked_example: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders; returns total rows. SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees; returns average of non-NULL salary values.
mistakes: Confusing COUNT(*) with COUNT(column) when NULLs exist
Using aggregate functions in WHERE instead of HAVING for group conditions
Assuming AVG includes NULL values in the same way as zeros
lessons.provenance: Authored original lesson; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

lessons.title: Scalar/String/Numeric Functions Basics
lessons.concept: Scalar functions operate on individual values and return a value per row. Common examples include string functions (UPPER, LOWER, LENGTH), numeric functions (ROUND, ABS), and date/time functions (depending on DBMS). Syntax and available functions can vary by database system.
lessons.formula: Examples: SELECT UPPER(name) FROM users; SELECT ROUND(price, 2) FROM products; SELECT LENGTH(title) FROM posts;
lessons.worked_example: SELECT UPPER('sql') returns 'SQL'. SELECT ROUND(12.345, 2) returns 12.35 (rounding behavior may vary by DBMS/settings).
mistakes: Assuming all function names/behaviors are identical across DBMSs
Applying string functions to incompatible types without conversion
Confusing scalar functions (per row) with aggregate functions (per group/set)
lessons.provenance: Authored original lesson; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

lessons.title: Using Functions in Queries
lessons.concept: Functions can be used in SELECT lists, WHERE clauses, ORDER BY, and other parts of queries (subject to rules). Using functions on indexed columns in WHERE may affect index usage in some cases. Aliases can make function results clearer.
lessons.formula: SELECT ROUND(salary,0) AS rounded_salary FROM employees WHERE UPPER(dept) = 'HR'; (index usage depends on DBMS/expression indexes)
lessons.worked_example: SELECT dept, COUNT(*) AS emp_count FROM employees GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(*) > 5; uses aggregate function in SELECT and HAVING.
mistakes: Placing group-level conditions in WHERE instead of HAVING
Forgetting aliases make results easier to read
Overusing functions in predicates without considering performance implications

questions.question: Which query correctly shows departments with more than 10 employees?

options.A: SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM employees WHERE COUNT(*) > 10 GROUP BY dept;
options.B: SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(*) > 10;
options.C: SELECT dept FROM employees HAVING COUNT(*) > 10;
options.D: SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY dept WHERE COUNT(*) > 10;

questions.explanation: Aggregate conditions on groups must be specified in HAVING after GROUP BY, not in WHERE.
